svg.title: Historic buildings provide a visual setting for a reading about contrasting experiences of an age.

text.tspan: Historic buildings provide a visual setting for a reading about contrasting experiences of an age.
It was the best of times, it
was the worst of times...
The narrator · Charles Dickens · A Tale of Two Cities, Book I,
Chapter I · Published 1859
Dickens opens his historical novel with a
sequence of apparent contradictions. The
narrator sets the opening in 1775, while also
comparing that period with the narrator's present.
Wisdom sits beside foolishness; hope beside
despair. This is narrative framing, not a recorded
public speech. Before introducing particular
characters, Dickens unsettles the idea that an
entire age can be summed up by one triumphant
or disastrous label. The opposing descriptions
prepare readers to notice how sharply
experiences can differ within the same society.
The repeated structure creates antithesis:
contrasting ideas are placed in parallel. The
effect questions sweeping judgments without
requiring either extreme to be wholly false.
How could both descriptions apply to the same
period without the narrator simply contradicting
himself?
